records.name: Vanuatu
records.current_summary: Vanuatu demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised); no LGR; small VPride community in Port Vila; kastom and church conservatism but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

sources.claim: Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

RNZ (18 Nov 2024): Parliament amended the Marriage Act to define marriage as the union of a male and a female; Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed same-sex marriages cannot be registered, and pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law.

RNZ (5 Nov 2024): Ministry of Justice and Community Services to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion; National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, framing V-Pride as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values — direct risk signal for visibly LGBT/trans visitors.

flags: 'Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised)' — regional sourcing indicates a 2007 penal reform equalised/removed prior offences; 'never criminalised' is wrong wording

records.name: Idaho
records.current_summary: Idaho carries the country's strictest criminalised restroom regime. Its 2026 facility-use law, effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching their birth sex — in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants and hospitals — with a misdemeanour of up to one year and a felony of up to five years on a repeat within five years. Four successive legislative rounds ran from 2023 to 2026, alongside a ban on official recognition of Pride flags.  A federal lawsuit followed the law's passage; contemporaneous reporting states the law was partially blocked, leaving it in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Since then a March 2026 bill extending felony restroom penalties to all public accommodations has passed the House, a March 2026 forced-outting statute has been signed, a birth-marker freeze has been in effect since January 2026, and the federation's Supreme Court declined in 2024 to review the state's bar on gender-affirming care.

sources.claim: ACLU of Idaho on HB 752: signed by the governor, effective 1 July 2026; makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching birth sex — in government buildings and any public-facing private business (gas stations, restaurants, entertainment venues, hospitals); first offence is a misdemeanour carrying up to a year in jail. The ACLU filed suit on 30 April 2026 arguing due-process, equal-protection and privacy violations, noting the law targets no actual criminal conduct.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (wire-service blocks automated fetch); the underlying national-wire article covers the legislature passing the transgender bathroom ban and jail threats, and the lawsuit that partially blocked it.

The 19th with Idaho Capital Sun, 30 April 2026: six transgender Idahoans sued to block HB 752 before its 1 July 2026 effect; the law is the only state law extending bathroom criminalisation to private businesses and carries steeper penalties than other states' bans (ACLU); suit challenges House Bill 752 as unconstitutional.

flags: court-blocked status claim rests only on 19thnews whose cached text covers the filing, not the outcome

freshness.fact: Claim understated, not stale: March 2026 felony bathroom bill (any public accommodation) passed House; March 2026 forced-outting law; Jan 2026 birth-marker freeze in effect; 2024 SCOTUS care-ban denial stands.

records.name: Louisiana
records.current_summary: Louisiana posts the country's highest measured killing rate against trans women: 24.7 per 100k trans women per year reported, 11.6 recorded, on the TGEU trans-murder-monitoring base (428 US victims, 2008–2025) — a floor rather than a total, though the same analysis cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and the top-ranked state records 23.5. In custody, a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence was killed by other inmates at Angola prison on 2 April 2024, at least the 16th violent death of a trans or gender-expansive person that year; killings continued into 2026.  On 31 May 2026 a mob of about ten beat a trans couple, Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders, outside a women's restroom at a park in Benton; no attacker was arrested, while both victims were charged with disturbing the peace and Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a female marker on her licence. On 15 July 2026 the Bossier Parish Police Jury unanimously approved — on the first of two required votes, reportedly at the sheriff's request — a local ordinance criminalising trans restroom use, described as one of the most punitive in the country. Louisiana has no statewide adult bathroom ban, so the parish ordinance is the state's sharpest instrument.

sources.claim: The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Louisiana records the highest per-capita killing rate of trans women of any state — 24.7 per 100k per year reported (19 recorded) against the top 'safest' state's 23.5 — on a base of 428 US victims 2008–2025; every figure is an undercount floor, and the piece cautions legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, with the worst-law states holding the highest rate.

Metro Weekly (Aug 2026): a mob beat trans couple Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders over restroom use at Cypress Black Bayou Park, Benton; Sanders (pre-existing spinal injury) and Rush (concussion, blood pooling) were both charged with disturbing the peace while no attacker was arrested; Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a 'female' marker on her driver's licence.

Erin in the Morning (5 Aug 2026): the same Benton mob attack — victims charged rather than their attackers, plea deal not signed; reports the municipality simultaneously voted one of the country's most severe anti-trans restroom ordinances; Rush was denied hospital care and taken to a men's jail, and no one else was arrested that day per the Sheriff's Office.

HRC memorial (11 June 2024): Yella (Robert) Clark Jr., a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence at Angola prison, was killed in a fight with several inmates on 2 April 2024 — at least the 16th trans or gender-expansive person HRC had learned of killed in 2024 and the fifth in April alone, with such deaths systematically under- or mis-reported.

flags: "first of two required votes" and sheriff-request detail not visible in caches (ordinance passage itself supported)

records.name: Texas
records.current_summary: Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.  Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

sources.claim: Texas Tribune (12 Dec 2025): SB 8 implementation — DPS troopers ID-checked people at women's restrooms outside the Capitol on 6 Dec 2025 (trans women holding female ID markers were admitted), the Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and opponents warn unclear guidelines produce uneven, invasive enforcement; protests followed at the Capitol.

Austin Current (27 Apr 2026): Attorney General Paxton's second complaint escalated the state probe of Austin ISD over bathroom policy, with a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint — the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry against a school district.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Texas carries the highest absolute toll of any state — 44 recorded killings of trans women 2008–2025, about 7.6 per 100k per year (undercount floor) — within the map's 'Do Not Travel' grading.

Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map, July 2026 update: Texas is one of four states in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers (with Florida, Idaho and Kansas), graded law-by-law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture by a five-year legislation-tracking methodology.

records.name: Tennessee
records.current_summary: Tennessee is the only US state with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere children could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable: the Sixth Circuit revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so its constitutionality has never been decided on the merits; no prosecutions are publicly reported, but a civil-rights suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event remains ongoing, and a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure rather than a dead-letter law.  Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters, and its ban on gender-affirming care for minors was constitutionally upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2025. Killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

sources.claim: LegalClarity (26 May 2026): the Adult Entertainment Act (2023, SB 3/HB 9) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — explicitly including 'male or female impersonators' — on public property or anywhere a child could see it; first offence is a Class A misdemeanour up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine, a second violation a Class E felony (1–6 years, fines to $3,000); it survived federal challenge on procedural grounds with a Supreme Court petition denied.

Advocate: the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to Tennessee's drag ban, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 Adult Entertainment Act in place; a separate suit remains ongoing, with performers saying they refuse to be silenced.

The Needle national analysis (July 2026, TGEU/Williams data): Tennessee's killing rate of trans women runs at 7.8 per 100k per year (10 recorded deaths, 2008–2025, undercount floor) and the state is graded in the 'Worst Laws Passed' tier — the record's comparative-violence figure rests on this piece.

freshness.fact: Drag-act SCOTUS litigation upheld the law; 2025-06-18 Skrmetti upheld minor-care ban; 2026 'Riley Gaines Act' adds birth-sex placement in prisons (and shelter ban) - facility claims current and expanding.

records.name: Kansas
records.current_summary: Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings, voids Kansas-issued IDs with corrected markers (licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified), and creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.  Two trans men sued within days of enactment (Doe v. State of Kansas, with civil-liberties counsel), citing fear of violence under the law; a May 2026 injunction covers only the healthcare provisions, leaving the facility and ID regime in force.

sources.claim: ACLU of Kansas SB 244 FAQ: the law confines trans people to birth-sex facilities with new civil and criminal penalties; bars updating driver's licences or state IDs and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex at birth — the Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice and many holders have already been told their licence is now invalid.

Erin in the Morning legal-risk assessment (20 Feb 2026): Kansas escalated Worst Laws -> Do Not Travel — the first 'Do Not Travel' state added in a year — driven by the new bathroom-bounty law letting private individuals sue trans people encountered in wrong-sex facilities; directly the assessment this record quotes on interstate-travel exposure.

records.name: Mississippi
records.current_summary: Mississippi enacted public-facility bans in 2024 and 2025 and defines legal sex by birth in statute, placing it in the worst-law group of the July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading.   One institutional counterweight is documented: a federal court sentenced the killer of a trans woman in Lucedale to 49 years for a bias-motivated murder — evidence that violence here can meet real prosecutorial response even while hostile law stands.

Mississippi Free Press/AP (23 Apr 2025): on 17 April 2025 the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled 8-1 that a transgender teen undergoing gender transition cannot change his name, denying a petition filed nearly two years earlier by a then-16-year-old whose parents both consented. The majority opinion, written by Justice James D. Maxwell II, referred to the trans boy as a 'minor female' and cited the 2023 REAP Act - which bans both surgical and non-surgical treatments for transgender minors - as Mississippi's express public policy against children receiving life-altering gender-transition assistance; a chancellor may grant a minor's name change only where clearly in the child's best interest. Dated state-court confirmation of Mississippi's judicial posture on gender-transition recognition.

Mississippi Free Press (1 May 2024): two anti-trans bills died in the Mississippi legislature after House and Senate lawmakers failed to reach agreement on compromise versions by the 29 April 2024 deadline - the 'SAFER Act,' which would have restricted transgender people's use of public bathrooms, locker rooms and public university dormitories (and which a House majority had previously supported), and the 'Women's Bill of Rights,' which would have codified a binary definition of sex as determined at birth into state law and curtailed legal recognition of transgender people's gender identities. Dated evidence of the 2024 legislative attempt at adult facility and sex-definition restrictions in Mississippi, which did not pass that session.

The Needle (16 Jul 2026), a state-by-state analysis of killings of trans women (per 100,000 trans women per year, 2008-2025, adjusted for undercounting): for Mississippi it records 6.6 such killings per 100,000 annually, above the US general-population homicide rate of 6.0 per 100,000 which the article prints as a comparison line; the piece's headline finding is that law tiers do not sort violence - both worst-law and safest-law states carry high rates. Gives the record a dated violence-rate datapoint for Mississippi, distinct from the state's legal-risk tier.
